lead: One path for the Mercor onsite design round, which Mercor describes as a backend system end to end: data model and schema, API, block diagrams, behaviour under concurrent load, recovery from failures and trade-offs. First the brush-up: which of your Accelerate sessions to redo or skim. Then the round itself: how to run the 45 minutes, and the designs it is reported to ask, drawn in full in the guide (a job scheduler, contractor payouts, ticket holds). The AI designs (candidate search, an AI interviewer) are optional now. Each topic: learn it, check yourself with multiple choice (say 'I don't know' when you don't, tick 'I'm guessing' when you are), explain the open question aloud, then compare and rate yourself.

modules.title: Brush up your system design
modules.blurb: Your own Accelerate sessions, in the order that pays most for the two reported prompts.

topics.title: System design brush-up from your plan
topics.brief: The Accelerate sessions to redo or skim before the onsite, in priority order. The backend design prompts Mercor is reported to ask (a job scheduler, contractor payouts, ticket holds) lean on the same few ideas: queues and backpressure, atomic claims, retries that are safe to repeat, and rate limits. Do the first four. Skim the next two. The rest is light.
points: Do first, w1a Throughput, latency, queues, backpressure: a scheduler is a queue with workers, and a search endpoint is a service under load. Both need a bound on the queue and a stated answer when it is full (shed load, reject, slow the producer). It also gives the p50 and p99 words to size things aloud

Do, w4e Transactions and indexes: how a worker claims a job with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so two workers never take the same row and never wait. Also the retry write with ON CONFLICT, the lost update and write skew anomalies, compare-and-set, and partial indexes for the queue and for failed jobs. This is the job scheduler's core

Do, w4a Things break at a hundred million: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, timeouts, dead-letter queues, and idempotency beyond payments. Every external call in both designs (a model, a customer API) fails sometimes, and 'what happens when it fails' is on Mercor's list

Do, w5e APIs and the edge: the token bucket, 429 with Retry-After, and idempotency keys on the front door. Rate limits matter twice here: protecting your service from tenants, and staying inside a model provider's limits
Skim, w4d Replication and consistency: leader and failover, fencing and consensus in outline. This is what sits behind 'only one scheduler instance may fire a job' and a lease that expires
Skim, w5f Streams and events: queue against log, at-least-once delivery, the outbox, dead-letter. Useful when a scheduler publishes events or a search index is fed by changes
Light review, w5a Caching: round 2 covered it. Reread the key terms and the stampede idea, which returns for cached embeddings and cached model calls
Skim if time, w2a How work splits and w3a Where a hundred million things live: hot keys and sharding for job ids and tenants, and back-of-envelope sizing for rows and vectors

links.label: w1a Throughput, latency, queues, backpressure (do)
links.why: Bounded queues and what to do when full. The vocabulary for both designs.

links.label: w4e Transactions and indexes (do)
links.why: Atomic claims with SKIP LOCKED, ON CONFLICT retries, partial indexes. The scheduler's core.

links.label: w4a Things break at a hundred million (do)
links.why: Backoff with jitter, timeouts, dead-letter, idempotency. Failure of every external call.

links.label: w5e APIs and the edge (do)
links.why: Token bucket, 429 and Retry-After, idempotency keys.

links.label: w4d Replication and consistency (skim)
links.why: Leader election, failover and fencing behind a lease.

links.label: w5f Streams and events (skim)
links.why: At-least-once, the outbox, dead-letter, replay.

links.label: w5a Caching (light review)
links.why: Round 2 covered it; keep the key terms warm.

links.label: w2a How work splits (skim if time)
links.why: Hot keys and sharding for job ids and tenants.

links.label: w3a Where a hundred million things live (skim if time)
links.why: Sizing rows, vectors and traces out loud.

mcq.q: Which two Accelerate sessions give the job scheduler its core: the atomic claim and the safe retry?
o: w2a and w3a
w4e and w4a
w5a and w5f
w1a and w5a
w4d and w5e
mcq.why: w4e has the SKIP LOCKED claim and the ON CONFLICT retry write; w4a has backoff, dead-letter and idempotency. The others support them.

modules.title: The system design round
modules.blurb: Mercor's backend round, end to end: how to run the 45 minutes, then the designs it is reported to ask, each drawn in full in the guide.

topics.title: How to run 45 minutes of backend design
topics.brief: Mercor describes the round as a backend system end to end for a realistic scenario, on a whiteboard, no code: data model and schema, API, block diagrams, behaviour under concurrent load, recovery from failures, trade-offs. This topic is the order and the clock. The designs after it are practice for the same order.
points: The order, from Mercor's own list: requirements and numbers, data model and schema, API, block diagram, the concurrency hazard, failure recovery, trade-offs. Follow it and say each name aloud, so the interviewer can see the structure

The minute plan, 45 in all. Requirements and numbers, 5. Data model and schema, 7. API, 5. Block diagram, built in stages, 8. The concurrency hazard, 8. Failure recovery, 8. Trade-offs and what you would do next, 4. Failure and concurrency get 16, because that is where the round is judged

Requirements and numbers (5 minutes): three functional requirements, what is out of scope, the delivery promise (at-least-once, with safe repeats), and the one or two numbers that change the design. Say that every number is an assumption. Do math only where it changes a decision

Data model and schema (7 minutes): the entities, which one is contended (many actors change it), money as integers in minor units, state as a column with legal moves, and the unique constraints that stop duplicates. Draw the tables with their keys, not a diagram of boxes

API (5 minutes): the write calls with an idempotency key, 202 and a status read for slow work, cursor pagination for lists, and the worker or provider side as its own small contract. Name the one field that makes retries safe

Block diagram (8 minutes): start with one node that works, name what breaks, and add one box at a time: a queue between choosing and doing, a worker pool, a sweeper, an outbox. State lives in the database; queues hold ids

The concurrency hazard (8 minutes): name it before you are asked. Two actors, one row. Pick the mechanism and say what the loser does: a unique constraint, a conditional update, SKIP LOCKED, a lease with a fencing token. Never hold a lock across a network call

Failure recovery (8 minutes): walk the arrows of the data flow and say what happens if the process dies on each one. Then the unknown outcome (a call that may or may not have happened), a sweeper that settles it, and a reconciliation that checks the books

Trade-offs (4 minutes): latency, cost, reliability, scalability, operational complexity, and what you would monitor. Say what you did not build and why. Mercor asks for why over tool names: justify each choice by the failure it prevents

Raise one failure case unprompted, state your numbers, and treat the interviewer as a collaborator: ask 'do you want me to go deeper here or move on?' at each stage. A collaborative conversation, not a performance
production: A design is judged on what happens when it breaks. The minutes spent on concurrency and failure are the ones that separate a passing answer from a diagram.

mcq.q: You have 45 minutes for a backend design. Which split puts the time where the round is judged?
o: 15 minutes requirements, 15 boxes, 15 on scale
5 requirements, 12 on schema and API, 8 on boxes, 16 on concurrency and failure, 4 on trade-offs
40 minutes of boxes, 5 for questions
20 on the schema, 20 on the API, 5 on the rest
All of it on scale math
mcq.why: Mercor lists concurrent load and recovery from failures as what the design is checked on. Requirements and schema are short and sharp; the failure minutes are the longest block after the diagram.

mcq.q: You have drawn the boxes and not mentioned concurrency. What do you do?
o: Say the database handles it
Name the row two actors both change, say what goes wrong, pick a mechanism, and say what the loser does
Add a global lock around everything
Put Redis in front and move on
Wait for the interviewer to ask
mcq.why: Naming the hazard first shows the design has no gap. A mechanism is a unique key, a conditional update, SKIP LOCKED or a lease with a fence, and the loser retries or skips.

open.q: You are given a backend prompt you have not seen. Walk me through how you spend the 45 minutes, and what you say at each stage.
open.probe: Where do the concurrency hazard and the failures come in, and how do you decide when to go deeper?
a: Requirements and numbers in 5 minutes: three functions, what is out, the delivery promise, one or two numbers that change the design.
Schema in 7 and API in 5: entities, the contended one, constraints for duplicates, an idempotency key on writes.
Boxes in 8, built in stages from one node: say what breaks, then add one thing.
Concurrency in 8 and failure in 8: name the hazard, pick the mechanism, walk each arrow for a crash, handle unknown outcomes, add a sweeper and a reconciliation.
Trade-offs in 4: latency, cost, reliability, operations, what I did not build and what I would watch. Ask the interviewer where to go deeper at each stage.

say: **I'll follow the order: requirements and numbers, schema, API, boxes, then concurrency and failure.**
**Before I draw:** the delivery promise, three functions, and the number that changes the design. Every number is an assumption.
**The schema first, not the boxes:** which entity is contended, money as integers, and the unique keys that stop a duplicate.
**I will name the concurrency hazard myself,** pick one mechanism, and say what the loser does. Then I walk each step and say what happens if the process dies there.
I'll finish with what I'd monitor, what I did not build, and why.
avoid: Starting with boxes and a database brand before the requirements and the schema.
Waiting to be asked about concurrency or failure.

topics.title: Design a distributed job scheduler
topics.brief: Reported as a 45 minute system design in the Mercor onsite (three reports). Run jobs now or at a time or on a schedule, across many workers, without losing one or running one twice by mistake. Open the design in the guide below; the lines above it say how Mercor tends to ask.
points: How it is asked: practical over theoretical. They want the tradeoffs on reliability, scale and operations, and what happens when a worker dies mid-job. Start with requirements and numbers, not boxes
The core loop: jobs are rows with a status and a time to run. A worker claims due jobs, runs them, and records the result. The claim must be atomic, so two workers never take the same job

Failure: a worker can die after taking a job. A lease with an expiry lets another worker take it back. Delivery is at-least-once, so jobs must be safe to run twice (idempotent), with a key they can check
Retries and limits: backoff with jitter, a retry cap, then a dead-letter state a person can look at. A per-tenant limit stops one customer from starving the rest

Scale: partition by job id or tenant, keep the due-jobs query on a partial index, and watch for a hot partition. A single scheduler that fires jobs needs a leader and a fencing token so a stale leader cannot fire twice
Operate it: queue age, lateness (start time minus due time), failure rate and retries as the dashboard. Late jobs, not CPU, are the user-facing symptom
production: Lateness, the gap between due time and start time, is the metric that pages someone; queue depth alone does not say whether jobs are on time.

mcq.q: Two workers poll the jobs table at the same moment. Which claim keeps them from taking the same job, without one waiting for the other?
o: Read the due rows, then update them by id in a second statement
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then mark them running in the same transaction
Lock the whole table while claiming
Add a random sleep before each poll
Run only one worker
mcq.why: Two statements leave a gap where both read the same rows. A table lock serialises every worker. SKIP LOCKED lets each take rows the other does not hold.

mcq.q: A worker takes a job, runs half of it and dies. What makes giving the job to another worker safe?
o: Exactly-once delivery from the queue
A lease that expires, plus a job that is idempotent and checks its key
Never retry, and alert a person
Run every job on two workers at once
Keep the worker's memory on disk
mcq.why: Delivery is at-least-once in practice, so the lease lets the job be reclaimed and idempotency makes a second run harmless.

open.q: Design a distributed job scheduler. Open with requirements, then walk the claim, a worker dying mid-job, and how you know jobs are running on time.
open.probe: What stops two workers running the same job, and what stops one customer starving the rest?
a: Requirements first: one-off and recurring jobs, how many per second, how late is too late, whether a job may run twice.
Claim: jobs are rows; a worker takes due rows with SKIP LOCKED in one short transaction and marks them running with a lease.
Failure: if the lease expires, another worker reclaims the job. Jobs are idempotent with a key, so a second run is harmless. Retries use backoff with jitter, then a dead-letter state.
Fairness and scale: a per-tenant limit, partitioned by tenant or job id, with the due query on a partial index. One scheduler leader fires recurring jobs, with a fencing token.
Operate: lateness, queue age, retries and failure rate on a dashboard, with an alert on lateness.

say: **I'd start with requirements and numbers, then the claim.**
**The claim:** jobs are rows, and a worker takes due ones with SKIP LOCKED so two never get the same job and none waits.
**A dying worker:** a lease expires and the job is reclaimed. Delivery is at-least-once, so jobs are idempotent and carry a key.
**Retries:** backoff with jitter, a cap, then a dead-letter state a person can inspect.
I'd watch lateness first, because that is what the user feels.
avoid: Promising exactly-once execution: say at-least-once with idempotent jobs.

topics.title: Design contractor payouts: a payment endpoint safe against timeouts, retries and crashes
topics.brief: Reported for Mercor as a charge-then-record payment endpoint, and as weekly payouts to thousands of contractors with an append-only ledger. Money moves in one system and the record lives in another, and no transaction covers both. Open the design in the guide below.
points: How it is asked: correctness under failure, not scale. The reported follow-ups are a crash between the charge and the record, a timeout where the outcome is unknown, retries, concurrent submissions, and whether one database transaction can cover the external call (it cannot)

The rule that decides the design: paying twice is worse than paying late. Commit the intent first (a payout row marked submitting), call the provider with the payout id as the idempotency key, then record the result, the ledger entries and the outbox event in one transaction

Unknown is a state. A timeout means the payment may or may not have happened. Look it up by key or by reference, or wait for the webhook, and move on only on a definite answer. Never retry with a new key after an unknown

Idempotency at every hop: the client's key at your door with a hash of the body, a unique key on contractor and period, the payout id to the provider, unique ledger rows per payout, and a processed-events check on webhooks

Concurrency: two batch runs or two workers go for one payout. A unique constraint and a conditional update decide the winner in the database. Do not hold a lock across the provider call; use a state with a lease

The ledger is append-only. A mistake is a reversal plus a new entry with a reason and an actor, and an overpayment becomes a balance to recover. A daily reconciliation against the provider's report, by key, is the check that does not trust anything else

Say the limit: if the provider has no idempotency key or no status lookup, automatic retry after an unknown is not safe. Put the payout id in the reference field, search by it, and send what is left to a person
production: A double payment found by reconciliation pages a person at once, and an unknown payout older than five minutes means the sweeper or the provider is stuck.

mcq.q: Your payout call to the provider times out. What state is the payout in?
o: Failed, so retry with a new key
Succeeded, so record it
Unknown: look it up by key or reference, or wait for the webhook
Cancelled, and tell the contractor
Delete the row and start again
mcq.why: A timeout does not say whether the money moved. A new key on a retry can pay twice. Only a definite answer from the provider moves the payout on.

mcq.q: Why not put the provider call inside the same database transaction as the payout record?
o: Transactions are slow in Postgres
The provider is not part of the commit: a rollback cannot unsend money, and the transaction holds locks across the network
Providers do not accept payments from transactions
It would save the record twice
There is no reason; it is fine for small payments
mcq.why: No transaction spans two systems. If the commit fails after the provider accepted, the money is gone with no record. Commit the intent first, then call, then record.

mcq.q: The weekly batch is run twice by mistake. What stops a second payout for the same week?
o: A check that no payout exists, run first
A unique key on contractor and period, plus a conditional update that attaches each hour to one payout
A comment in the runbook
Running the batch only at night
Paying in smaller amounts
mcq.why: A check-then-insert lets both runs pass the check. The unique key and the conditional update decide in the database, where the decision is atomic.

open.q: Design a payment endpoint that is safe against timeouts, retries and crashes. Start from the failures: what can go wrong between charging the provider and writing your own record?
open.probe: What is the state after a timeout, and what does the system do when it finds a payout stuck in that state?
a: The failure: money moves in the provider and the record is in my database, and nothing commits both. A crash between the two leaves money moved and no record.
Fix: commit a payout row as submitting first, call the provider with the payout id as the idempotency key, then record the result, the ledger entries and an outbox event in one transaction.
Unknown: a timeout is unknown, not failed. A sweeper looks the payment up by key or reference, and the webhook tells me too. A new key only after a confirmed failure.
Concurrency: a unique key on contractor and period, a conditional update for the claim, a lease for a dead worker, a fence on the record. No lock across the call.
Audit: an append-only ledger, corrections as reversals, and a daily reconciliation against the provider's report. Page on a double payment.

say: **The problem is that the provider and my database cannot commit together.** So I commit the intent first, as a payout in submitting.
**Then I call the provider with the payout id as the key,** and record the result, the ledger entries and the outbox row in one transaction. A crash in any window leaves a row for a sweeper to check.
**A timeout is unknown, not failed.** I look it up by key, or wait for the webhook, and only a definite answer moves it on.

**Duplicates are stopped where they are atomic:** a unique key on contractor and period, and a conditional update. The ledger is append-only, and a daily reconciliation checks it against the provider.
If the provider has no key or no status lookup, I do not retry automatically. I search by reference and send the rest to a person.
avoid: Promising exactly-once: say at-least-once attempts with one key and an at-most-once effect, and say where it depends on the provider.
Claiming payments experience you do not have. Say the discipline you do have: a record of intent before an outside call, keys, and a way to find out what happened.

topics.title: Ticketmaster: contention and holds
topics.brief: The classic baseline for two workers or two buyers wanting the same thing. The job scheduler's duplicate-run problem is the same contention: a conditional update, a hold with an expiry, a lock with a lease.
points: Read the deep dives on holding a seat and on the queue in front of a hot event.
Carry over: a conditional update or a lease decides who wins; the loser retries or moves on.
Say it in the scheduler: a job is claimed the way a seat is held, with an expiry so a dead worker gives it back.

Holds: a seat is held with an expiry (a status and a time, or a Redis lock with a TTL), never by keeping a database lock open for the whole checkout. The expiry gives the seat back when a buyer walks away.

Double booking: the database is the backstop. A conditional update or optimistic concurrency means only one buyer's write succeeds, even if the hold layer fails. The loser is told and offered another seat.

Payment uncertainty: the same unknown outcome as in contractor payouts. The booking carries a key, the payment webhook is handled idempotently, and a hold that that expires while a payment is in flight is reconciled, not guessed.

mcq.q: Buyers hold a seat while they pay, which can take minutes. What is the right way to hold it?
o: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat for the whole checkout
A status and an expiry (or a lock with a TTL), with a conditional update at confirmation as the backstop
No hold; whoever pays first wins and the rest get refunds
Lock the whole event
Hold the seat in browser storage
mcq.why: A database lock held for minutes ties up connections and leaks if the buyer leaves. A hold with an expiry gives the seat back on its own, and the conditional update at the end keeps the sale correct even if the hold layer fails.

open.q: Design the booking path for a high-demand event so a seat is never sold twice. What happens when a buyer's payment outcome is unknown?
open.probe: What holds the seat, what is the backstop if the hold layer fails, and what does the loser see?
a: A hold: the seat gets a status and an expiry when a buyer starts checkout, so an abandoned checkout gives it back.
A backstop: confirming is a conditional update on the seat, so only one buyer's write succeeds even if the hold layer is down.
Payment: the booking has a key, the payment webhook is idempotent, and an unknown outcome is looked up, not guessed.
Spikes: a waiting queue in front of the hot event, and a clear message to the loser.

say: **A seat is held with an expiry, not locked for the whole checkout.**
**The database is the backstop:** confirming is a conditional update, so only one buyer wins even if the hold layer fails.
**A payment that times out is unknown.** The booking has a key and the webhook is idempotent, so I look it up instead of guessing.
For a hot on-sale I'd put a waiting queue in front and tell the loser plainly.
avoid: Keeping a database row lock open while a person types a card number.

topics.title: Other prompts reported
topics.brief: Four more prompts reported for the Mercor backend round, each with a core hazard and a first move. A few lines each, so you recognise the shape in the room and reach for the right guide technique. Not full designs.
points: Social feed (stable pagination, deletions, privacy). Hazard: pages that shift while posts are added or removed, so a reader sees duplicates or skips, and a deleted or private post that keeps showing from a cache. Move: cursor pagination on (created_at, id) instead of offsets; fan out on write for normal accounts and on read for huge ones; check privacy and deletion at read time against the source of truth, with tombstones so caches drop the post

Dataset deep copy (a dataset with its tasks, responses and grades). Hazard: a duplicate copy request, a worker that dies half way, a stale worker that wakes up and writes, and edits during the copy. Move: an idempotency key on the request, a background job with checkpoints and a stored old-to-new id map, a claim with an expiring lease and a fencing token, the copy hidden until a final atomic flip, and cleanup for failed copies

Check-and-insert for about a million IDs (latency, memory, accuracy). Hazard: check-then-insert is a race, so two requests both see 'not there' and both insert. Move: the database unique key is the truth, with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A hash set of a million 8-byte IDs is about 8 MB and fits in memory; a Bloom filter (about 1.2 MB at a 1% false-positive rate) only skips lookups for IDs that are surely new, and never replaces the constraint

Project-to-contractor matching (hard eligibility, capacity, cold start, feedback). Hazard: two projects take the same contractor's last free hours, and new contractors with no history never get shown. Move: hard filters first (skills, availability, rate, region), then a ranked top-k; reserve capacity with a conditional update so only one project wins the hours; leave room for exploration of new contractors; feed outcomes back and evaluate on a held-out set

The common move: find the row two actors both change, put the decision in the database (unique key, conditional update, lease with a fence), make every retry safe with a key, and say what the loser does
production: In each of these the quiet failure is a duplicate or a stale copy that no error reports, so the design needs an invariant check or reconciliation, not only error alerts.

mcq.q: You must check whether an ID exists and insert it if not, for about a million IDs and many concurrent requests. What is the safest core?
o: SELECT, then INSERT if the row is missing
A unique key and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, with a Bloom filter only as an optional shortcut
A Bloom filter alone
An in-memory set on each server
A global lock on the table
mcq.why: Check-then-insert is a race. The unique key decides atomically and is exact. A Bloom filter has false positives, so it can skip lookups for new IDs but cannot be the answer.

mcq.q: A deep copy of a large dataset is claimed by a worker that then stalls for a minute. A second worker takes over. What stops the first one from corrupting the copy when it wakes up?
o: Nothing; the last writer wins
A fencing token: every claim bumps a number, and writes must present the current one
A longer lease
Running the copy twice and keeping the better result
Locking the source dataset
mcq.why: A lease alone cannot tell a paused holder from a dead one. The fence is checked where the write lands, so the stale worker is rejected.

open.q: Pick one of these: a social feed, a deep copy of a dataset, check-and-insert for a million IDs, or matching projects to contractors. Name the core hazard and your first move.
open.probe: What does the loser of the race see, and which part of your answer would break if a retry arrived twice?
a: Feed: shifting pages and deleted content that stays visible. Cursor pagination, privacy and deletion checked at read time.
Deep copy: duplicates, dead and stale workers, edits during the copy. Idempotency key, checkpoints with an id map, a lease with a fence, a hidden copy and an atomic flip.
Check-and-insert: a race on check-then-insert. A unique key with ON CONFLICT is the truth; a Bloom filter is a shortcut.
Matching: two projects take the same hours. Hard filters, ranked top-k, capacity reserved by a conditional update, exploration for new contractors.

say: **For any of these I look for the row two actors both change,** and put the decision in the database.
**A feed:** cursor pagination so pages do not shift, and privacy and deletion checked at read time.
**A deep copy:** an idempotency key, a background job with checkpoints, a lease with a fence, and the copy hidden until a final atomic flip.
**Check-and-insert:** a unique key with ON CONFLICT. A Bloom filter only saves lookups and never replaces it.
**Matching:** hard filters, ranked top-k, and capacity reserved with a conditional update.
avoid: Using a Bloom filter or an in-memory set as the source of truth for uniqueness.

topics.title: Design candidate search for a job description
topics.brief: Reported both as a 45 minute system design and as a 90 minute build against an evaluation endpoint. Given a job description, return the best candidates from a large pool, and know how good the results are.
points: How it is asked: practical, about AI systems: retrieval, evaluation, model behaviour, failure modes, monitoring. Open with requirements and the numbers (how many candidates, queries per day, how fresh), then the shape

The shape: filters on hard facts, then keyword and embedding retrieval fused, then a rerank of a short list, with an LLM used where it is worth the cost (extracting fields, rewriting the query, explaining a match)

Cost and latency: cheap stages cover the whole pool, expensive stages see only the top few dozen. Embeddings are computed once per profile and refreshed on change; per-query model calls are counted and capped
Evaluation is half the design: a labelled set of jobs and good candidates, precision at 5 and recall, a held-out slice, and failures read by hand. Without it you cannot say a change helped

Failure modes: a wrong hard filter drops the right person, keyword stuffing wins, a model invents a skill during extraction, stale profiles rank first, a bias in the labels becomes a bias in the results

In production: monitor result click and hire signals, score drift after a model change, latency by stage, and the share of queries with no good result. Roll out a new ranker behind a comparison on real queries
For the build version of this, see wc38; for the design checklist, wc36
production: A new ranker or embedding model is rolled out against the old one on the same queries first, because a silent model update moves every score.

mcq.q: You can afford an LLM call on about 50 candidates per query, from a pool of 100,000. Where does the LLM go?
o: On every candidate, once per query
On the top 50 from a cheap stage, to rerank or explain them
Only on the job description, never on candidates
On a random sample of 50
Nowhere; LLMs cannot rank
mcq.why: The cheap stages (filters, keywords, embeddings) cover the pool; the expensive model sees only the short list, where order matters most.

mcq.q: Your tuning score keeps rising but a held-out set of jobs does not move. What does that suggest?
o: The held-out set is broken
You are overfitting to the tuning data
The model needs more parameters
Precision at 5 is the wrong metric
Nothing; only the tuning score matters
mcq.why: Gains that do not carry to unseen jobs mean the change fits the tuning data, not the problem.

open.q: Design candidate search: a recruiter pastes a job description and wants the best candidates. How do you build it, and how do you know it works?
open.probe: Where does the LLM earn its cost, and what is your evaluation set?
a: Requirements and numbers: pool size, queries a day, freshness, how bad a miss is.
Shape: hard filters, then keyword plus embeddings fused, then a rerank of the top few dozen. LLM extraction of fields and query rewriting where messy text hides the signal.
Cost: embed each profile once and refresh on change; cap model calls per query; cache.
Evaluation: labelled jobs and candidates, precision at 5 and recall, a held-out slice, failures read by hand.
Failures and monitoring: wrong filters, keyword stuffing, invented skills, stale profiles; watch score drift and the no-good-result rate.

say: **I'd start with the pool size and what a miss costs, then the shape.**
**The shape:** filters, then keywords and embeddings together, then a rerank on the short list. The LLM goes where it earns its cost.
**Evaluation:** a labelled set with a held-out slice, and I read the failures by hand. In MetaRAG I measured retrieval changes the same way.
**Failures:** a wrong filter, keyword stuffing, an invented skill, stale profiles.
And I'd compare a new ranker to the old on the same queries before it ships.
avoid: Calling a toy label set a benchmark, or claiming a gain that was not measured.

topics.title: Design an AI interviewer with rubric grading
topics.brief: A design taken from what Mercor sells (wc36): an AI that asks a candidate questions, listens, follows up and grades the answers against a rubric. It is not reported as an onsite prompt, so treat it as likely practice for the AI-systems design round.
points: How it would be asked: practical, about model behaviour, evaluation and failure modes. Start with who uses the grade and what a wrong grade costs, then the pipeline

The pipeline: a rubric of named criteria, a question flow that can follow up, a transcript, a grader that scores each criterion with evidence from the transcript, and a human review path for low-confidence or high-stakes cases
Grade one criterion at a time, with its own prompt, a short scale with written anchors, and a quote as evidence. One broad 'rate this candidate' call is vague and unstable
Trusting the grader: compare it with human graders on a labelled sample, measure agreement per criterion, and repeat the same answer to measure consistency. Fix the rubric text before the model

Failure modes: a long confident answer scores high, bias by accent or style, prompt injection from the candidate's answer, a cheating candidate reading from another tool, and a grader that drifts after a model update

Cost, latency and ops: a live conversation needs fast turns, grading can run after the call in a queue, and every grade stores the rubric version, the model version and the evidence so it can be replayed and audited
For the design checklist and the other three Mercor-style designs, see wc36
production: Every grade stores the rubric version, model version and transcript evidence, so a disputed grade can be replayed and a rubric change can be tested against past interviews.

mcq.q: How do you decide whether an LLM grader can be trusted with a rubric?
o: If it gives confident explanations
Compare its scores with human graders on a labelled sample and measure agreement per criterion
If it uses the largest model available
If it scores the same on a second run, whatever the humans think
You cannot; use only humans
mcq.why: Agreement with human labels is the test. Consistency alone can mean consistently wrong, and confidence is not evidence.

mcq.q: The same answer gets 3 on one run and 5 on another. What do you fix first?
o: Switch to a bigger model
Tighten the rubric: separate criteria, a short scale with written anchors, and require quoted evidence
Average ten runs and hide the spread
Remove the rubric and let the model decide
Ignore it; scores vary
mcq.why: Vague criteria cause unstable grades. Anchors and per-criterion prompts fix the cause; averaging only hides it.

open.q: Design an AI interviewer that grades candidates against a rubric. How do you make the grades trustworthy?
open.probe: How do you know the grader agrees with a human, and what happens on a low-confidence grade?
a: Who uses the grade and what a wrong one costs, to set the bar.
Pipeline: rubric, question flow with follow-ups, transcript, a grader per criterion with quoted evidence, and a human review path.
Trust: compare with human graders on a labelled sample, measure agreement per criterion, measure repeat consistency, and fix the rubric text first.
Failures: confident long answers, style bias, prompt injection in an answer, cheating, drift after a model update.
Ops: grade after the call in a queue, store rubric and model versions and evidence, replay old interviews to test a change.

say: **I'd start with what a wrong grade costs, then the pipeline.**
**One criterion at a time:** a short scale with written anchors and a quote as evidence, not one broad rating.

**Trust the grader by measuring it:** agreement with human graders on a labelled sample, and the same answer repeated for consistency. In MetaRAG I built an automated evaluation framework the same way.
**Failures:** a long confident answer, style bias, injection from an answer, drift after a model update.
Low-confidence and high-stakes grades go to a person, with the evidence attached.
avoid: Saying the grader is accurate without a human-labelled sample to show it.
